details:
MarsAtlas: An Integrated Martian Terrain Intelligence & EVA Traverse Planning System

Summary

MarsAtlas is an experimental planetary exploration and geospatial decision-support platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map." Focused on Jezero Crater, Mars, the platform brings together planetary mapping context, real Perseverance rover exploration records, prototype terrain analysis and computational A* traverse planning. Users can examine terrain-related characteristics, explore scientific context and compare alternative routes under different exploration priorities. MarsAtlas demonstrates how planetary observations and computational methods can support more interpretable exploration decisions. It is an experimental research prototype, not a certified astronaut safety or operational mission-planning system.

Project Details

1. The Problem We Address

Robotic missions have generated extensive scientific observations of Mars, including orbital imagery, elevation models, geological maps, mineralogical observations, rover traverses and surface imagery.

However, these datasets differ in spatial resolution, coordinate systems, coverage, scientific purpose and acquisition time.

For future human exploration, viewing surface imagery alone is insufficient. Explorers need to understand terrain characteristics, examine available scientific observations, identify potential destinations and compare alternative routes.

The central challenge is therefore not simply the availability of Martian maps. It is the difficulty of interpreting different planetary observations together in an exploration-oriented workflow.

2. Our Approach

MarsAtlas addresses this challenge through an integrated planetary exploration environment.

The platform organizes available mapping context, rover exploration records, prototype terrain information and computational route planning around a common exploration workflow.

Users can:

  • Explore the selected Martian region.
  • Examine available planetary mapping context.
  • Inspect rover waypoints and traverse records.
  • Investigate terrain-related characteristics.
  • Compare alternative computational traverse strategies.
  • Examine geological context and science-interest locations.

The primary study region is Jezero Crater, the landing and exploration region of NASA's Perseverance rover.

Jezero's crater floor, delta region, surrounding terrain and geological diversity make it an interesting setting for investigating the relationship between planetary terrain and scientific exploration.

3. Planetary Data and Exploration Records

MarsAtlas uses a combination of planetary mapping resources, rover exploration records and manually prepared scientific context.

Planetary Mapping Context

The application provides a planetary mapping environment for exploring the selected Martian region.

The available basemap and mapping resources are used to establish geographic context for terrain inspection and route exploration.

Perseverance Rover Records

MarsAtlas uses NASA-AMMOS MMGIS Perseverance waypoint and traverse datasets.

The existing project documentation reports 708 Perseverance waypoints and 559 traverse legs across Sols 13–2022. These counts describe the dataset used by the project and are subject to the coverage of the source records.

These records provide real robotic exploration context for the Jezero region.

Curiosity Comparative Context

Curiosity waypoint records provide additional comparative exploration context from Gale Crater.

They are not treated as part of the primary Jezero traverse analysis.

Rover Surface Imagery

The application uses NASA Mars 2020 Raw Images API resources alongside curated image references and fallback behaviour.

These resources help connect geographic exploration with available rover surface observations.

Geological Context

Five simplified geological polygons provide approximate geological context based on Sun and Stack (2020), USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3464.

These are manually simplified overlays and should not be interpreted as a complete authoritative geological map.

Science-Interest Locations

MarsAtlas includes five manually authored CRISM-referenced science-interest locations.

These locations provide contextual targets for science-priority route exploration.

The current implementation does not independently process CRISM spectral cubes, perform mineral classification or independently detect mineral deposits.

Documented but Not Integrated Resources

The project documents additional scientific resources, including:

  • Mars Trek CTX and THEMIS mapping services.
  • Mars 2020 HiRISE Digital Terrain Model products.

These resources are potential sources for future development. Their documentation does not mean they are currently integrated into the active frontend map or terrain-planning pipeline.

The distinction between operational application data, manually authored context and documented external resources is maintained throughout the project.

4. Terrain Intelligence

A major component of MarsAtlas is the computational interpretation of terrain characteristics.

The current route-planning workflow uses a prototype surrogate terrain grid named jezero_eva_sector.npz.

Its documented characteristics are:

  • Grid dimensions: 550 × 350 cells.
  • Approximate cell spacing: 11.3 × 11.9 metres.
  • Primary study area: a selected sector of Jezero Crater.

This grid is a prototype surrogate. It is not a validated terrain crop directly derived from the raw 1-metre HiRISE DTM.

The terrain workflow considers:

Elevation: Represents the vertical position of terrain within the prototype grid.

Slope: Estimates local terrain gradient using Horn's 3 × 3 finite-difference method after Gaussian smoothing.

Local Roughness: Uses local elevation standard deviation to represent variations in the surrounding terrain.

Terrain Factor: Combines selected terrain-related factors, including roughness and thermal-inertia-related proxy values, within a computational model.

The implementation accounts for Mars' reference radius of approximately 3,396,190 metres when converting planetary angular coordinates into approximate horizontal distances, including latitude-dependent longitudinal scaling.

The project documentation reports an exploratory comparison against 276 Perseverance waypoint elevations, with an RMSE of approximately 74 metres and a mean bias of +55 metres.

This comparison is an exploratory consistency check, not independent scientific validation. Differences may arise from the surrogate grid, vertical reference systems, waypoint localization, spatial sampling and other data uncertainties.

Terrain indicators should not be interpreted as direct measurements of soil bearing strength, traction, rock distribution or astronaut-scale surface safety.

5. EVA Traverse Planning

MarsAtlas uses an eight-connected A* search algorithm to compare potential exploration routes across the prototype terrain grid.

The algorithm considers eight neighbouring directions when exploring possible paths.

Unlike a purely shortest-distance calculation, the implemented route cost incorporates several terrain and exploration-related factors.

The cost function is:

c = max(0.05, wE·E_hat + wT·T_hat + wS·(θ/10)² + wH·max(0, (250−TI)/100) − wV·min(0.6, V)) × d/10

Where:

  • E_hat represents the normalized energy-related traversal cost.
  • T_hat represents the normalized time-related traversal cost.
  • θ represents local terrain slope.
  • TI represents the thermal-inertia-related terrain input.
  • V represents the science-target preference contribution.
  • d represents movement distance.
  • wE, wT, wS, wH and wV are configurable weighting parameters.

The planner uses three weighting configurations:

Lower-Slope Preference: Gives greater importance to slope-related penalties.

Balanced Preference: Emphasizes a balance between estimated traversal effort and time-related costs.

Science Priority: Assigns greater importance to proximity to selected science-interest locations.

The current planner excludes grid cells exceeding its configured 22-degree slope threshold. This is an implementation constraint, not a universal astronaut safety limit.

The resulting route distances, times and energy-related estimates are illustrative computational outputs generated using the prototype terrain representation and simplified modelling assumptions.

They are not validated predictions of astronaut performance, operational EVA requirements or certified safety assessments.

6. Science Along the Traverse

MarsAtlas treats exploration as more than movement between two geographic coordinates.

Scientific context can influence which locations are worth investigating.

The platform connects route exploration with available rover records, approximate geological context and manually authored CRISM-referenced science-interest locations.

This enables users to examine potential destinations and understand their contextual scientific relevance.

The application distinguishes between real mission observations and interpretive or manually authored overlays.

7. Integrated Exploration Workflow

MarsAtlas organizes planetary exploration into a sequence of connected tasks:

  1. Select the exploration region.
  2. Inspect the available planetary mapping context.
  3. Examine terrain-related characteristics.
  4. Select a starting location and destination.
  5. Compare alternative A* traverse strategies.
  6. Investigate science-interest locations and rover observations.
  7. Review the resulting route information and its underlying assumptions.

This workflow demonstrates how geospatial visualization, terrain indicators and computational pathfinding can support comparative planetary exploration.

8. Technical Architecture

MarsAtlas uses a modular web-based architecture.

Frontend

Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS provide the web application interface.

Geospatial Visualization

OpenLayers 9 provides interactive planetary mapping capabilities. Three.js supports local three-dimensional terrain visualization where implemented.

Backend

Python 3.11 and FastAPI provide the computational service layer.

Scientific Computing

NumPy and SciPy support numerical processing and terrain calculations. Rasterio supports geospatial raster-processing workflows.

Pathfinding

A custom eight-connected A* implementation evaluates alternative traverse paths using configurable terrain and exploration-related costs.

Deployment

The frontend is deployed using Vercel, with backend services hosted through Render.

The application is an independently developed experimental prototype.

9. Scientific Reliability and Limitations

MarsAtlas distinguishes between real mission observations, computationally derived indicators, manually authored context and simplified modelling assumptions.

Its principal limitations include:

  • The active route-planning terrain grid is a prototype surrogate rather than a validated raw HiRISE-derived terrain model.
  • CTX and THEMIS WMTS resources and the raw HiRISE DTM are documented but not integrated into the active frontend map implementation.
  • Geological polygons are simplified and approximate.
  • CRISM-referenced science-interest locations are manually authored; independent spectral processing and mineral detection are not implemented.
  • Terrain roughness does not establish soil bearing strength or traction.
  • Thermal inertia is not a direct measurement of surface traversability.
  • The route planner uses simplified computational assumptions.
  • The configured slope threshold is an algorithmic constraint, not a universal safety threshold.
  • Any radiation-related values are illustrative proxies, not Jezero-specific dose predictions.
  • The platform does not provide validated astronaut physiological, PLSS, cooling, oxygen or EVA safety calculations.

MarsAtlas is therefore an experimental planetary exploration and decision-support prototype, not an operational NASA mission-planning system or certified astronaut safety assessment.

10. Intended Impact

MarsAtlas demonstrates a practical approach to connecting planetary mapping context, rover exploration records, terrain-related computation and science-informed route comparison.

Its central contribution is an exploration-oriented workflow that helps users investigate how different terrain and scientific priorities can influence computational traverse recommendations.

The broader objective is to make planetary observations more interpretable and demonstrate how geospatial software and computational pathfinding could contribute to future human surface exploration research.

MarsAtlas is independently developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and does not imply official NASA endorsement.

NASA and Scientific Data References

Data and Mission Resources

  1. NASA Mars Trek — Planetary Mapping API documentation.
  2. NASA Mars 2020 — Perseverance Waypoint Dataset.
  3. NASA Mars 2020 — Raw Images API.
  4. NASA Mars 2020 — Perseverance Mission.
  5. NASA-AMMOS MMGIS — Rover mapping and exploration records.
  6. Sun and Stack (2020) — USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3464, Geologic Map of Jezero Crater and Nili Planum.

Software and Engineering Resources

  1. OpenLayers — Geospatial mapping library.
  2. FastAPI — Backend framework.
  3. NumPy — Numerical computing.
  4. SciPy — Scientific computing.
  5. Rasterio — Geospatial raster processing.
  6. Three.js — 3D visualization.
  7. GitHub — MarsAtlas source code.

Additional resources such as HiRISE DTM, CTX, THEMIS and CRISM are documented as potential future integration sources and are not represented as operationally integrated datasets.
